job.style: a comparison of two related ideas

passage: In the Chola Empire, administration was organized into groups of villages known as a Nadu, which functioned as the primary unit of local governance. These village settlements, called Ur, were not just residential areas but hubs of economic activity where local councils managed irrigation and land revenue. Unlike the belief that kings managed every local detail, the Chola administration relied on these village councils to handle daily affairs, including the maintenance of water tanks and canals. These irrigation systems were carefully planned by the community to ensure agricultural success, rather than relying on natural rainfall alone. Chola temples served as much more than places of worship; they were the core of social and cultural life, acting as centers for craft production and education. Skilled artisans worked within these temple complexes to create exquisite bronze statues. While many of these statues depicted deities, artists also crafted realistic figures of royal patrons and devotees, showcasing the diverse artistic talent of the period. The king’s power was often displayed through his patronage of these temples, which served as symbols of his authority and wealth. By delegating authority to local councils and investing in public infrastructure like irrigation, the Chola kings maintained a stable and prosperous kingdom that thrived through organized community effort.

items.evidence: In the Chola Empire, administration was organized into groups of villages known as a Nadu, which functioned as the primary unit of local governance.
items.q: In Chola administration, what exactly was a Nadu?
options: Several villages joined together as one unit
A small neighbourhood inside a single village
A council that ruled the whole empire
A separate country ruled by a samanta
items.explain: A Nadu was a group of villages and the main unit of local government.

wrong.why: thinks a Nadu was a part of one village
thinks a local unit ruled the empire
thinks local areas were independent kingdoms

items.evidence: Unlike the belief that kings managed every local detail, the Chola administration relied on these village councils to handle daily affairs, including the maintenance of water tanks and canals.
items.q: A village tank in the Chola kingdom starts leaking. Who would most likely arrange its repair?
options: The local council of that village
The king, who decided every matter himself
The temple artisans who made bronze statues
The council of the Ur ruling the empire
items.explain: Chola kings relied on village councils for daily work like looking after tanks and canals.

wrong.why: thinks the king handled every local matter
picks a nearby group named in the passage
thinks the Ur ruled the whole empire

items.evidence: These irrigation systems were carefully planned by the community to ensure agricultural success, rather than relying on natural rainfall alone.
items.q: Why did Chola farmers not have to depend on rainfall alone?
options: The community had planned its own water systems
Water reached the fields naturally without effort
The king personally decided each field's water
Temple priests prayed for rain every season
items.explain: Villagers carefully planned irrigation together, so farming did not depend only on rain.

wrong.why: thinks temples were only for worship

items.evidence: Chola temples served as much more than places of worship; they were the core of social and cultural life, acting as centers for craft production and education.
items.q: Which example shows that a Chola temple was more than a place of prayer?
options: Children studied and craftsmen worked inside it
Priests held daily prayers and festivals inside it
The Ur council governed the whole empire inside it
Kings planned attacks on other faiths inside it
items.explain: Chola temples were centres of education and craft production, not just worship.

wrong.why: thinks temples were only for worship
thinks the Ur ruled the empire
links temples only to religious hatred

items.evidence: While many of these statues depicted deities, artists also crafted realistic figures of royal patrons and devotees, showcasing the diverse artistic talent of the period.
items.q: A Chola bronze shows a lifelike man in royal clothes. Who could it show?
options: A royal patron who supported the temple
A god, since bronzes showed only deities
A samanta who ruled his own country
A Mughal ruler from the Tripartite struggle
items.explain: Besides gods, Chola artists made realistic bronzes of royal patrons and devotees.

wrong.why: wrongly places the Mughals in this period
